content: GIVING up alcohol for a month has a dramatic effect on health, lowering blood pressure, cholesterol and risk. It can also drastically reduce levels of cancer-related protens in the blcui, according to the first wide-ranging study of tie benefits of of abstinence like "Dry January".

The study involved 141 drinkers. On average, they drank morethan double the UK recommended limit, consuming around 30 units a week — the equivalent of atxut three of wine or more than 14 pints Of beer.

For the study, 94 Of them gave up drinking for a month, whie the rest continued to dnnk as usual. A team at the Royal Fræ Hospital in London analysed samples taken at the start and end Of the month from each participant.
The people who carried on drinking showed no particular changes over the course of the month. The abstainers, however, displayed big improvements.

confirming those reported in a small study of 14New Scientist staff in 2013. The most striking change was in insulin resistance. This when the hormone insulin becomes less effective at making the body remove sugar from the raising the risk of ty pe 2 diabetes.

After a month, abstainers saw their insulin resistance fall by an average Of 26 per cent. "Our data suggest that alcohol use recommended guidance markedly Increases the risk ot 2 says Gautam Mehta of U niversity College London, who led the team together with his colleague Kevin The abstainers also saw improvements in liver health plus an average 13 cent fall in cholesterol levels, a 6 per cent drop in blood pressure, and a 1.5 cent decline in weight (BMI O'æn, doi.org/cpms).

"Over one month, that's as much as you could hovæ to lose if you were dieting " says Mehta. Surprisingly, the team also found a dramatic drop in the Of two growth factors "After a month without alcohol, there was a dramatic drop in growth factors linked to cancer" linked to One, vascular endothelial growth factor, helps tumours grow by building networks of vessels. After a month of levels of this substance in the fell by 41 per cent. There was also an average drop Of 74 in levels of epidermal growth factor, which promotes cancer growth by encouraging cells to multiply.

"The reductions were very striking," says Mehta. "They fell in almost every abstaining participant," he says. "They are Only correlations at this stage, but deserve further investigation," says Ketan Patel of the MRC Laboratory Of Molecular Biology in Cambridge. UK The evidence that drinking leads to cancer is well -pstahlishpd and overwhelming. he says. The question is by what mechanism." Mehta suggests that alcohol may help push small tumours to progress i nto more serious cancer.
Although the study included a comparison group that to drink, one limitation is that the all knew whether they were in the control group or the drinking group.

Unsurprisingly, it's difficult to do experiments where the participants don't know if they are drinking alcohol or not. In theory, those who abstain from drinking may influenced by a placebo effect, or unknowingly feel encouraged to pursue other healthy lifestyle changes in the course of the study, distorting the results.
However, Mehta says that the team did not see any changes in participants' lifestyles, diets and exercise regimes during the study.

Despite the observed of a month's abstinence, Mehta warns that should not aq_qump that their hOdy and are fully "detoxed " and ready for bouts of excessive drinking after doing Dry January. The findings are very but we don't know how long they last, he says.

However, the act of abstaining for a time seems to also have a effect on drinking habits. When the researchers contacted the abstainers around seven months later, they found that they were drinking 20 per cent less alcohol on average than they used to.
"It shows if you have a month ott, It can reset your relationship with alcohol long-term," says Nick Sheron at the University of Southampton, UK u 19 May z0181Newscjentist17

They called It the "Remicade high The medicine works by bbcking a signalling molecule in called TNF. It was designed to calm the inflammation behind arthritis, so why should it affect people's This puzzling observation is just one clue that the State af enhanced immune activity we call inflammation could also depression, argues Edward Bulimore in The Inflamed Mind.

Depression is the most common mental illness. but our existing antidepressant treatments are inadequate. A new understanding would Bullmore 's take On depression is fascinating and provocative, but it didn't leave me feeling that the case is closed. The standard explanation is that depression is caused by some sort of imbalance of the chemicals used by brain cells, such as serotonin. Antidepressantslike Prozac serotonin levels.
But these medicines aren't very effective — indeed, for many, they don •t work at all — so It mks Mental stress causes inflammation. Can this lead to depression?
461 Newscientist 130 June 2018 as ifwe are missing something. Most of us know inflammation as something affecting a small part of the For instance.
if we cut our it tE•cornes red, swollen and painful. This is when immune cells rush to the area and release compounds to fight Off invading bacteria. It also encourages us to rest our injured limb.

There is also a state of slightly raised immune activity called systemic inflammation. This was first identified in clearly inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, but it txcurs more widely beca use it ha s been linked to obesity and ageing — as well as psychological stress.

The intriguing idea at the heart Of this is that mental adversity causes inflammation. which then causes depression. This mechanism might even be helpful — provided it dæsn't "Even if inflammation isn't the grand theory of everything, understanding it would be a real advance" persist for too long— because it makes us want to crawl away and rest our whole body, removing us from the stress.

Bullmore takes us on a tour Of the growing evidence sup1K)rting this idea, such as studies showing that under stress have higher levels Of inflammatory molecules in their blcxxl, as do people with depression.

A psychiatrist at the University of Cambridge. Bullrnore skilfully interleaves tales of his patients with the science. But for me, it rings false when he implies that objections to the idea stem from the outdated Cartesian view that the mind exists outside the physical realm, so its maladies could not have physical causes.

psychiatrists are happy enough to treat depression With the very physical remedy of prozac. And while Bullmore makes a case that inflammation causes depression, if anythiny his advocacy is strong. I would have preferred a more impartial account of the evidence, for and against. According to sorne studies, only a third of people with depression have raised levels of inflammation — so where does that leave everyone else?

Still. even if inflammation isn't the grand theory of everything that Bullmore would like it to be, understanding the role it dcæs play would a real advance. Bullmore for a future when blcxxi tests can indicate whether people have "inflamed depression" and, ifthey do, they will receive anti-inflammatories, including some of Rxlay's arthritis medicines, rather than Prozac.

Despite my caveats. anyone interested in how the mind works will enjoy this : With concerns growing ov•er the risks and benefits ot exastmg antidepressants, this isone area that desperately needs an infusion Of new ideas. •

Just a month or earlier, Hanna-Attisha had been urging the children in her care to drink the water in place of unhealthy sugary drinks — she felt it was her duty as an asscxiate professor at MSU's College of Medicine in Flint and a paediatrician in the city's Hurley Medical Center. content: the EPA considers water with high lead concentration to hazardous, this historical confusion seems to linger. If she was to change minds, Hanna-Attisha realised she would need ev idence that lead levels in the Of Flint residents had risen after the water switch.

The clock was ticking: thotsands of people were drinking Flint river water. But getting access to such data can take years. When a similar crisis played out in Washington DC in the early 2000s, Marc Edwards of Virginia Tech in Blacksburg was only *'le to show that lead IN)isoning had occurred four years after the crisis ended.

But Hanna-Attisha is a dcxtor and the Hurley Medical Center tests the blood lead levels of Flint's children as part of routine healthcare. She already had the data. She and her team worked mund the "We checked, we double-checked, we triple- checked, we quadruple-checked this data," she says, and the results wereclear.

The ofchildren with high levels of lead in their blood had risen significantly following the change in water supply. On 21 she went to the local authorities with her results, but she says they seemed unwilling to act. Attisha felt she had no choice but to go public. As the hour Of the press conference approached, the room filled with journalists and camera crews. Flanked by her team, Hanna-Attisha remembers her voice sounding calm and assured — even as her heart thudded in her "When the entire state is telling you you're wrong... it is hard not to believe them" chest. She had felt like the holder of an awful secret, and it was a relief to set it By early evening she was national news.

Instead of congratulated for her work, however, she found herself under attack. A spokesperson for the Michigan Department of Environmental Quality called her conclusions "unfortunate" in a time of "near hysteria". The State governors Office went further, saying Hanna-Attisha's team had "spliced and diced" the data. "That was definitely the lowest pint," she says. "When the entire state is telling you you're wrong, that feels like crap. And it's hard not to believe them at a certain point." Days passed. Hanna-Attisha says she was sick with worry. What if she was wrong and worrying people needlessly? Or, worse, she was right and nothing was going to Then. suddenly, the Icyal authority declared a public health emergency. On 1 October it announced that residents should drink tx)ttled water or use water filters. Significantly, some reporters had analysed figures the state had released to counter Hanna-Attisha's findings and found that they actually supported her claims. Her conclusions were accepted.

A fortnight later, Flint was reconnected to Ihtroit's water supply — something the state had months claiming wasn' t feasible. It was just 52 days since Hanna-Attisha had become aware of the lead problem.

The full impact of the crisis remains to be seen. research suggests there was a rise in Flint's miscarriage rate during the water came from the Flint nver. Other studies - link the improperly treated water to an outbreak Of Legionnaire's in which 12 people died. Some people connected with the Flint water crisis may face charges of involuntary manslaughter. And there are still concerns around Flint's water: all Of the lead pipes need replacing, and that has not yet happened.

Lead exposure causes rprmanent damage. The only option is to try to mitigate its effects, and that is where Hanna-Attisha is directing her attention. When I visit, she takes me on a tour of the Hurley centre. It's an ultra-modern, Olourful SIYICe, and is where she now leads the Pediatric Public Health Initiative. a multi- pronged project to provide as much health and social support as possible for Flint's children. Although the parents coming and going from the centre with their children just like parents everywhere, Hanna-Attisha says that below the surface they are angry — and anxious about what the future holds.

Whatever that may there is no doubt Hanna-Attisha 's intervention prevented an even worse situation. When Washington had its lead problem, the people drank the water for more than three years. "It felt like I was the right at the right time in the right place and with the right team," she says. • Colin Barras is a science writer in Ann Artl)r, Mthiqan. content: Simply changing your attitude could make you fitter, slimmer, less stressed and even younger, finds David Robson UR minds aren 't passive observers simply observing reality as it is; our minds actually change reality.

The reality we experience tomorrow is partly the prcxiuct ofthe mindsets we hold tcxlay." Tha€s what Alia Crum told global movers and shakers at this year's World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzærland. It may sound like New Age but Crum, who heads the Mind & Bcxiy lab at Stanford University in California, can back up her claims with hard evidence showing the mysterious influence the mind has over our health and well-being.

Crum's pioneering research was inspired by her own experiences as a child gymnast and college ice hcxkey player. "You can be the same physical day tn tho ru•vt." says, "but your mindset can have a dramatic effect on performance and physiological capabilities." She often wondered why.

Then, as a psychology student, she read atx•ut the placel:x:' effect and had a eureka moment : if our expectations can influence the effectiveness of a drug, something similar can in other situations, Pursuing that idea, Crum and others have discovered that your mindset affects everything from your weight and fitness to tl•w physical toll of insomnia and stress — even how well you age. The upshot is that two could have identical genes and lifestyles but one can end up healthier than the other, thanks solely to their ditterent thoughts.

Plac&s are inert pills used in most clinical drug trials. The participants are divided rancbrnly into two groups: half take the drug being tested, the rest, for comparison, take an identical-looking sugar pill. With no active ingredient, the placetk) shouldn't have any effects. Yet it often brings about measurable changes, the release of natural and lowering pressure, for example — all because of people's expectations. Patients sometimes reap these benefits even when they know they are taking the placebo (see " Everyday placTtx)s", page 30).
On the downside. our expectations of a pill can also produce side effects, including nausea and skin rashes. This is the plac& effect's "evil" twin, the effect (see "The science page 32).

Crum was "blown away" when she leamed hnw powerful can "Rut what surprised me most was the fact that we 've done relatively little to understand and harness them to improve health and well- " she says. Governments spend huge amounts of money encouraging us to adopt healthier lifestyles. What if our efforts could be boosted, or undermined, by the very psychological processes that influence a drug's efficacy through the and effects, Crum wondered. content: It might seem surprising that a mouth bacterium has been in Alzheimer's disease (see main story). But it wouldn't the first time an illness has turned Out to have an infectious origin.

The iconic case is stom.uh ulcers, once thought to catsed by stress or excess and with medications. Then Australian doctor Barry Marshall showed that a stomach called Helicobacter Wlori was them. a feal that won him a Nobel prize.

Streptococcus bacteria, which cause tonsillitis and "strep throat'. are of tri"ering obsessive-compulsive disorder in children. The thinking is that the immune systems on the bacteria cross-reacts with certain human proteins. causing an autoimmune attack against the own brain tissue.

arefft the only ones under suspicion. There are indications that a virus is behind some cases of And one study has found that with to a single-celled brain parasite called Toxoplasma gondii. which is in cat faeces. are more I ikely to develop schizophrenia. Some think up to a third of cases could be caused by infection with T. gondii.

But not all purported links bear fruit. Twenty years ago. there was great excitement when a bacterium that can cause pneumonia lung infe•ctions was found in the vessel plaques that cause heart disease. But giving people antibiotics to kill this bug didn't help reduce heart attacks.

Clare Wilson We don't know how P gingivalis gets into the brain, but there areplausible routes it could take. Your mouth normally hosts a diverse and relatively stable community of bacteria, but when dental plaque builds under the edge of your gums, it can form inflamed pcxkets in which p.gingivalis can thrive and release toxir%.

This inflammation can to chronic and tooth loss (see " Everything you need to know about gum disease", page 7). and some studies have shown that people with fewer teeth are more likely to have dementia. The inflammaticn and toxins caused by P gingival's damage the lining of your mouth, which may make it possible for oral bacteria to enter the bloodstream and then other organs. Even if you don't have gum disease, transient damage to your mouth lining from eating or tooth- brushing can let mouth bacteria into your blood, says Lynch.

The blood-brain barrier should protect your brain from microbes, but P. gingivalis can invade white cells and the cells lining vessels, so might cross it that way. It may also invade cranial nerves near the mouth, then spread from cell to cell towards the brain over a Of years.

As to how P gingivalis might cause dementia atter it arnyes in the brain, there are two clear rxssibilities. It may trigger the release ofamyloid, the brain's method Of trying to 81 NewScientist 1 2 February 2019 "This is why years of efforts to treat Alzheimer's haue seen few results" Porphyromonas oinoivolis is the main bacterium in gum disease contain the infection, and this may then kill neurons.

Or P gingivalis may directly damage the brain. We already know that Alzheimer's involves inflammation, an excessive immune response that ends up killing neurons instead of protecting them. P. gingiva/is is known to cause inflammation in gum tissue, and it may do so in the brain as well.

In response to the new findings, David Reynolds ofthe Alzheimer's UK charity said he is dubious that P gingivalis causes Alzheimer's, because Of the evidence showing that a genes play a crucial role in the disease. "Strong genetic evidence indicates that factors other than bacterial infections are central to the development of Alzheimer's, so these new findings need to be taken in the context Of this existing research," he said in a statement.

But a bacterial hypothesis for Alzheimer's doesn 't conflict with genetic evidence. The human body's propensity for inflammation can vary according to genetic variations that affect our immune systems, and this may influence how much damage P gingivalis induces in a brain.

The biggest genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's is a variant of the gene that makes the APOE immune protein. Last year, a team in Sweden found that the gingipains released by P. gingivalis break up the APOE protein into fragments, cleaving it at the site of a particular amino acid within the protein, and that these fragments may harm nerves. The AB)E4 variant of this protein contains more of this amino acid, suggesting that the reason people who make this variant are at a higher risk of developing Alzheimeds may tm•ause harmful levels ot APOE protein fragments build up more quickly in their brains than in those of other Hope for treatments The speed at which damage accumulates is a key factor in the disease. Although many people harlX)ur P. gingivalis in their mouths, only some develop Alzheimer's. Because it can be decades before Alzheimer's symptoms appear, whether a person develops the condition could ome down to how much damage cwcurs before they die of other causes.

"Alzheimer's strikes people who accumulate gingipains and damage in the brain fast enough to develop symptoms during their lifetimes," says Lynch. She says her team's findings are a "universal hym)thesis of pathogenesis", fully explaining the causes of Alzheimer's disease.

But Vissel warns that Alzheimer's is a complex disease. "The answer is unlikely to be one-cause-fits-all. We need to keep eyes." However, the new study is "very exciting", he says. "Alzheimer's is so common in people at advanced age that I think it can only be either some intrinsic property Of the brain, or an infection."

A vaccine for gum disease would welcome — and if it also stops Alzheimer's the impact could enormous. It is early days for this new hypothesis, and if the pursuit of amyloid-busting drugs over the past few decades has taught us anything, says Vissel, it is that a complex disease may nol have a simple mechanism.
Even if P. gingivalis is confirmed as a cause of Alzheimer's. we don't know yet whether it will turn out to be the only cause or one of several factors contributing to the disease.

"This is very important," says George Perry at the University of Texas at San Antonio. "The view that pathogens might one of several paths leading to Alzheimer's disease fits my current thoughts of amyloid and tau being critical brain responses to injury, instead of the initiators." That, he says, is why years of efforts to treat Alzheimer's by removing those proteins have seen few results: they are symptoms of the disease, not its cause.

But the problem rema ins complex. Paul Ewa ld cautions that we need to look at the interplay among factors rather than simple causal chains. And notes that Western lifestyles have altered so much and so fast —a prcress that is ongoing — that pinpinting the changes involved in cancer won't be simple.

The news is that we may already have the information we need. Every year, large. costly studies are launched to try to determine whether a certain substance or Ik•haviour is carcinogenic. content: THE shared ancestor of every organism now on the planet lived at least 3-9 billion years ago— adding weight to theories that life started 100 million years earlier than we thought, at a time when Earth was still pummeled by meteorites.

That's according to a study that has combined genetic and fossil evidence to build a timeline ofcrucial shifts in the early evolution of life. The study also sheds new light on the birth cf complex cells, which today make up all animals and plants.

For the first few billion years or Earth's history, the only lite present was single-celled microorgani _ U the hrge plants and animals that in the past 600 million years, such as trilobites and dinosaurs, these microtrs left few fossil; — so understanding life's early history has tricky.

To find out more, Holly Betts at the University Of Bristol, and her colleagues combined two sources of evidence. They compared the sequences of 29 genes across 102 tc build a family tree that showed how they were all related, and the order in which new groups split away from their relatives.

The researchers then added some dates to this tree, taken from the geological record. This enabled them to estimate when the various groups evolved and parted company. For instance, they knew that life could be Older than 4-52 billion years because that is when a rock the size of Mars slammed into Earth, forming the moon. The impact was so severe that the planet's entire surface melted. "Nothing could have survived it," says team member Davide Pisani. also the University of Bristol.

The result is a tirneline of the first 3 billion years of life, from the ancestor of all modern life to the first complex animals (Nature Ecology & Evolution, can go very "This is the best attempt yet to actually get a coherent picture of the history of life on Earth" deep in time, which we never thought was says Pisani.
"I think they've really made the most sincere and honest effort yet to actually get a coherent picture of the history of life," says Bill Martin at the University of Düsseldorf in Germany.

One major finding is that the most recent organism that all existing life is related to — known as the last universal common ancestor, or LUCA— lived at least 3-9 billion years ago. There is tentative support for life to have existed this early in our planet's history. Some have suggested that traces of carlx»n in 4.1-billion- year-old rocks are signs of early life. Similar traces were found in 3-95-billion-year-old rocks in 2017.
And another 2017 study claimed to have found fossilised single- celled organisms from 3-77 billion years ago. But all these findings are disputed.

Nevertheless, Greg Fournier at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology says the new date for LUCA is reasonable. This means life probably formed relatively quickly, within 600 million years Of the mcx»n-creating impact, when big meteorites were still battering the planet.
Supercharged life LUCA gave rise to two groups Of single-celled micrcX)rganisms called bacteria and archaea. This split happened at least 3-4 billion years ago, the study finds.

Later on, more-complex cells evolved — one Of the most crucial evolutionary events ever. Compared with bacteria and archaea, these "eukaryote" cells Early Earth may not have been as inhospitable as we thought are larger, with compartments and tiny, energy- supplying mitochondria.
All animals, plants and fungi are eukaryotes, and if these cells had not evolved, we could never have existed. The timeline suggests these cells first appeared at least 1.84 billion years ago.

It was thought that eukaryotes evolved in to rising oxygen levels, but this finding suggests this might not have the case, as the first atmospheric oxygen turned up much earlier — 2.4 billion years ago. However, it does not rule Out a link, as there was little oxygen at first and levels later rose in fits and starts.
The timing of the eukaryotes' origin is curious it place almost exactly when the study found that microtRs called alphaproteobacteria evolved.
The mitck•hondria inside eukaryotic cells were once free- living alphaproteobacteria, which were somehow swallowed by an archaean that then gave rise to the first eukaryotes.
The implication is that acquiring mitochondria was the key Step in eukaryote evolution, says Pisani. This then spurred a massive evolution of diversity among eukaryotic cells, he says.

Martin and his colleagues have made a similar argument on physical grounds, suggesting that the first eukaryotes could Only have evolved large, complex cells once they had mitochondria to supercharge them.

However, Fournier suspects the timings might be off. He says are quite different from their alphaproteobacteria ancestors, "so they should be substantially younger". • 25 August 20181 NewScientist 1 5

But as the Spanish hpgan tn take nvpr tho Inca empi rp and impose their own customs, they equally enthralled by the way the scxiety was organised.

The Incas governed the 10 million people in their realm with what amounted to a federal system. Power was centred in Cusco, in the south ofwhat is now Peru. but spread through several levels of hierarchy across a series of partially self-goveming provinces.

"Break the khipu code and we might finally read an indigenous Inca history" was no money and nc market economy. The production and distribution Of food and othercommodities was ce controlled. People had theil own land to farm, but every subject was also issued with necessities from state storehouses in exchange for labour, administered through an impressive tribute system.

Historians have argued variously that the Inca empire was a sociaist utopia or an authoritarian monarchy. But no one disputes its efficiency. True, he was prone to ambiguity and contradictions. But about a third ofthe khipus in collections to have a more elaborate construction than the others, as if they contain a different sort of information.

For decades the EX)int was however, because no one could read any of them. The first hints of revelatior_s from khipus came in the 1920s, when anthropologist Leland Locke analysed a bunch of them housed at the American Museum of Natural History in New York. He noticed that the knots arc organised in rows a,most like beads on an abacus (see diagram, page 37).

He demonstrated that each row of knots at a certain height denoted units, tens, hundreds and so on. That made sense, fitting with the decimal system the Inca used to divide up groups for tribute purposes Hard knot to crack The discovery sparked a wave of interest in khipus. By the 1990s, though, we still had no idea what the meant. "Say you read off the number 76 - what dcB it refer to? asks Urton.

To answer that, you would ideally have a translation of a khipu into a familiar language. It would be an equivalent of the Rosetta stone, which a translation of Egyptian hieroglyphics into ancient Greek and unlcxked that picture language. In the absence Of that, Urton has spent the last 25 years tracking down and carefully digitising the details of every khipu he could find in museums and private collections across the world. Today, his Khipu Database Project contains details of more than of them.

There are all sorts of varying factors in khipus: the colour ofthe strings, the structure Of the knots and the direction in which they were hitched. Having spent countless hours poring over them, Orton began to think that binary differences in these features might encoding information. For example, a basic knot tied in one direction could moan " paid" while in the other it would mean "unpaid" By 2012, he had developed a more specific hypothesis, proposing that the direction in which knots were tied, the colours of the strings, or some combination of the two, corresponded to the scrial status of the people whose tributes they recorded, and even individuals' names. Without a khipu translation, however, the idea destined to remain untested.

content: archaeological dig Alison George THE extensive archaeological dig in Europe is underway in the UK, thanks to the high-speed train line built between Birmingham and London (see map). Major construction projects like the new line, known as HS2, are an ideal to investigate the buried past.

building work this year, archaeologists will investigate River Trent Birmingham River Avon 60 different sites along the 240-kilometre route _ The digs will uncover 10,000 years of history, from the time of hunter-gatherers through to the Roman, Saxon, medieval and modern eras. "We expect to find archaeology from every period in our history," says Mike Court, the lead archaeologist on the project.
Here are Of the highlights. 118TH-CENTURY BURIAL GROUND Birmingham This Industrial Revolution-era graveyard is thought to hold more than 10,000 and 1500 have recovered so far.

The skeletal remains will tell us the effects of 18th and 19th-century life on those living in Birmingham. One intriguing finding is that some of the skeletons show evidence of dissection — probably by students at a nearby medical schcx»l in operation at the same time as the burial ground.
Boddington Edgecote Great Ouse 2 IRON AGETOSAXONERA SITE Boddington Before any digs began, the route of HS2 was surveyed using laser scanners and magnetic detectors.

"These techniques give a map of what's going on underground," gays Court. They have thrown up surprises, including in what "Major construction projects like the UK's HS2 train line are an ideal opportunity to study the buried past" like an uninteresting field near the village Of Bcxldington in Warwickshire.

•Ihe field wasn't thought to have been crcupied in the past, but the surveys revealed a large Bronze Age or Iron Age structure, and others that appear to Roman and Saxon, suggesting it may have used for over 1000 years.

"If we find towns and settlements where we thought there weren't any, that's what this project is about," says Court. 3 WAR OF THE ROSES BATTLEFIELD Edgecote The HS2 route runs close to the site of a key battle in the English civil war known as the War Of the Roses. The battle took place on 26 July 1469.
Aside from accounts by Welsh not much is known about this battle, so archaeologists are hoping to uncover arrowheads, wearx)ns and lx•ssibly mass burial pits to figure out how it unfolded.

Birmingham Curzon St Brmingham Irterchange London St Mary's Church Grim'; Ditch River Colne Calne Valley London 4 MEDIEVAL BURIALGROUND St Marys Church, Stoke Mandeville Possibly the most interesting medieval site along the HS2 route is the graveyard of the demolished church of St Mary's in the village of Stoke Mandeville. Between 3000 and 5000 bodies were interred here, starting around the 12th century.

It is an unprecedented opportunity to investigate the population of a village over a long time says Court. "There's a gocxi chance that we'll find burials due to the Black Death and Of plague." 5 BRONZE AGE DYKE GrimS Ditch This long, deep ditch on the outskirts of London is thought to have been constructed in the Bronze Age or Iron Age, but we don't know why it was built.
"We're hoping to solve the mystery of Grim 's Ditch," says Court. It could mark the tx•undary of an ancient territory, or perhaps the route of migratory animals.

6 STONE AGE HUNTER- Colne Valley GATHERER SITE The Colne Valley on the outskirts of London may have been an imiMtant place for the nomadic hunter-gatherer people living in Britain 10,000 years ago. At that time, low sea levels meant Britain was connected to mainland and archaeologists think that the Colne Valley may have been a migration route from Europe via river systems.
They will looking for gravel areas in the river which might have been used by these ancient as they followed animal herds.

"If we're really lucky we might find a butchery site, where they tcxjk down an animal like a mammoth," says Court, though that is probably unlikely. "I'd happy if we find any evidence of human activity." 161 NewScientist 1 5 January 2019

content: OST accounts of life on Earth tpgin little more than half a billion years ago. That is when an evolutionary burst of creativity produced the ancestors of alrncßt all animals and plants alive today. Following this "Cambrian explosion" , life's story is one of fish, amphibians, insects, land plants, the rise and fall of the dinosaurs, and ultimately the emergence Of humans. It is an epic tale — but it spans just one-eighth of life's history.

The problem is that although animals and plants have left abundant fossils, Precambrian rocks contain almost no traces of earlier life. This vexed Charles Darwin, who wrote in On the Origin of Species: "To the question why we do not find records of these vast primordial I can give no satisfætory answer." Since then, a few fossilised remains have found, but these are mostly micros«vic reluctant to give up their secrets. Yet, in recent years, ingenious researchers have found new ways to lift the lid on life's black box.

This is the story of the firs: 3-5 billion years. It is a tale dominated by single-celled organisms, but it is also oneofcataclysrnic change. It encompasses thebirth of the continents, the greatest act Df chemical pollution ever committed, znd a freak evolutionary event that mav never have happened anywhere else in the universe.

It is an epic Journey, so buckle up. In the was Earth. It formed some 4-54 billion years ago from rocks and dust and, soon afterwards, was smack•d in the face by 281 Newsoentist | 12 January 2019 another baby planet (or several small ones) _ The impact melted Earth's surface and threw chunks of matter into orbit, forming the moon. Where one vital ingredient for life, Earth's water, came from is a long-running debate. It may have med up in the that formed the planet, been brought in later by comet, or perhaps it came from interstellar space and is older than the sun itself.

"Life might have been easier to get going than was once thought" Exactly when life got started isn't clear. "The oldest uncontroversial evidence we have is the Pilbara Strelley Pool stromatolites," says Greg Fournier of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Found in Western Australia, these preserved mats of microorganisms are 3-4 billion years Old. They cannot the first life, though, the cells have complex membrane structures and link together into chains. They like "a complex, diversified bacterial ecosystem", says Fournier.

Claims of older fossils are regularly touted. And the earliest known chemical traces Of life appear to date from 4.1 billion years ago. But this evidence is controversial, partly Earth is thought to have Ipen battered by meteorites between 4 and 3.g billion years ago, rendering it uninhabitable. However, over the past few years, this "late heavy tx»mbardment" was reassessed. Simulations suggested that rather than happening in one short, sustained blast, large meteorites kept hitting at a low rate until about 3 billion years ago. These impacts would have caused problems for life, but couldn't have obliterated it.

That helps explain why there was little pushback this August, when a new calculation put the origins of life firmly before 3.8 billion years ago. Davide Pisani at the University Of Bristol, 0K, and his colleagues compiled genetic data from JOZ living species and built a family tree showing how they were related.

Then they took some firm dates from the fossil record and used these to work out how fast evolution has been happening, allowing them to estimate when some of the key stages in the history of life One of these was theorigin of the last universal common ancestor (LUCA), which they calculated lived at least 3-9 billion years ago.

The very first organisms would have arisen even earlier — remarkably near the start Of Earth's history —hinting that life might have been easier to get going than once thought. We already have some idea of what LUCA was like. Several teams have used genetic methods similar to Pisani's to figure out which genes it had and which evolved later.

Nevertheless, oxygen helped one ofthe most dramatic events in Earth's history; an ice age so severe that all (or almost al) the planet froze over. This first "snowball Earth" shortly after oxygen in the air, and lasted until 2.1 billion years ago. Atmospheric oxygen played a part by reacting with the methane prcxluced by methanogens, reducing the chemical 's greenhouse effect. A second cause was the emergence of the first large continents (see "A short history of rcxks", page 32). paler than the seas, they reflected more Of the sun's heat back into space. Finally, chemical reactions associated with the weathering of newly formed nountain ranges removed another greenhouse gas, dioxide, from the air.

We tend to think of oxygenas being essential for life, but in the beginning it was a deadly form or pollution, and its accumulation in the air probably caused the first mass extinction. Tachy, oxygen is toxic to "anaerotæs" — organisms that live in places — so it was presumably lethal to many ancient microbes, says Fournier. The ice on snowball Earth would also have destroyed many habitats. However, the microbial fossil record is too to show this. "There is no way to empirically detecta microbial mass extinction. he says.

Not so boring billion Following this chilling upheaval came a of calm — or so we thought. Conventional wisdom has it that, with the climate stable and oxygen levels low, evolution stalled. Life's history was considered dull that the 1.8 billion and million years ago has been the " txjring billion". In fact, it was nothing ofthe sort. This is when life made two Of its biggest advances. And, according to recent research, these evolutionary innovations may have been the result of organisms rising to the challenge of coping with limited nutrients.

Whatever the reason, the first big leap was the emergence Of a new kind Of organism, called a eukaryote. Pisani 's study estimates that this between 1.8 and 1.2 billion years ago, deep in the billion.

Eukaryotic cells are larger and more intricate than anything that came before. They have complex internal membranes, their DNA is stored in a charntrr called a nucleus, and they contain tiny. sausage-shaped objects called mitcxhondria that supply them with energy.

Only eukaryotic cells can form complex, multicellular organisms like plants, insects and humans - bacterial and archaeal cells cannot link up in such fiddly ways — so the origin of eukaryotes is one of the most important events in the history of life.

Eukaryotes arose not through which drives so much Of evolution, but by ccx•peration. At some point, an archaean must have swallowed a bacterium and the two organisms managed to live as one, with the bacterium the first mitcxhondrion.

Quite how this happened is still debated. We may know more by studying a recently discovered group or organisms called the Asgard archaea, which are the closest simple-celled relatives Of eukaryotes _ However, the creation of complex life seems 12 January 2019 | Newsaentist | 31

They then began a slow dance called the supercontinent cycle. Every few hundred million years, the coninents all collided to form One gigantic land mass. Columbia was probably the first existing between 2.1 and 1.5 billion years followed, from about 1.3 billion to 750 million years And the last was Pangaea, which existed during the dinosaur era.

With the evolution of eukaryotes, life on Earth could take another big leap and become multicellular. when did that happen? Until the 1950s, the oldest known multicellular organisms were from the Cambrian period, which started 541 million years ago. Then some English schcx)lchildren discovered a fossil, which was the first recognised Ediacaran, a weird, multicellular organism that lived between 635 and "Perhaps evolution was slowed when Earth turned into a giant snowball" 542 million years ago. The nature of this group has long been a mystery. A new study suggests that at least one of them, called Dickinsonia, was an animal — the earliest known, at half a billion years old. Ediacarans weren't, however, the first multicellular organisms.

In 2016, a team led by Shixing Zhu of the China Geological Survey described rectangular and tongue-shaped blobs that were up to 30 centimetres in length. They look like primitive seaweed and were found in Chinese rocks dated at 1.56 billion years old. Fragments of preserved cellular material revealed the Dickinsonia (left) may the oldest known animal. Stromatolites (right) are far Older but not the first life on Earth cells to be organised in tightly packed sheets, not in colonies, strongly suggesting they were true multicellular organisms. This year, a follow-up study found that, until 1.57 billion years ago, the where those organisms lived was low in oxygen, then levels rose, that it was the extra oxygen that enabled them to grow larger and more complex.

People used to wonder why multicellular organisms so long to evolve. Now we have a new puzzle : Why it took them a billion years to develop into the more complex forms of the Ediacarans. Perhaps oxygen levels had to rise still further. Or perhaps evolution was slowed in its tracks by a second snowball Earth that occurred between 720 and 635 million years ago. However, the microfossil record shows little evidence Of out at that time. Indeed, it has argued that some organisms thrived on Earth's icy surface.

so, mysteries still remain. Life's Dark Ages have yet to be fully illuminated. But we know far more than we did just a few years ago. And it is clear that life as we know it today would not exist without all the innovations that happened in the first 3-5 billion years of evolution.

This previously unknown animal comes from 600-millbn- year-old rocks in China and doesn't have a name yet. While Dickinsonia was an Ediacaran — a primitive group of organismsthat went extinct about 541 million years ago — the unnamed animal seems to have belonged to a group of animals that still exists tocay: comb Jellies.

It was discovered by Zhenång She at the China University of Geosciences, Wuhan. "The orgin and earliest evolution of animals is a fascinating question that has puzzled scientists for many decades," said She as he unveiled his findings at a meeting of the Geological Scxiety of Londonin London last week.

The fossils were found in a drill core taken from the Doushartuo Formation in M)uthern China have already yielded exquisitely preserved fossils :rom as far back as 631 million years ago. Among these rcxks, She's torn has found fossils visible to the eye, measuring 0.7 millimetres across. The first clue to their identity was their jellyfish-like shape. Microsccvic analysis revealed what appear to tentacles, muscle tissue nerve cells, gonads, mucous layers and clusters or hairlike structures called cilia.

True jellyfish belong to the Cnidaria phylum Of animals, but She said these features are reminiscent of the comb jelly phylum Ctenophora. The cilia clusters in particular look like structures called ctenes that comb jellies use to swim.

fossils most closely resemble the living genus of comb jellies called Pleurobrachia, or sea goos&rries, She told the meeting. Nonetheless, comb jellies would remarkably advanced for 600 million years ago, says Tim Lenton at the University Of Exeter, one Of the organisers. Living comb jellies have a gut connecting their mouth and anus, a feature not present in many Other primitive groups including the Cnidarians.

If the new fossils are comb jellies, more discnvprips may yet be to come. The vast majority Of living comb jellies today are predators, feeding on small marine organisms. They resemble algae, he says. The discovery has yet to be or published in a journal but has been seen by other scientists, said She.

The comb-jellylike structures could artefacts or bacterial contamination, he says. If it does check out, the discovery won't radically alter Our knowledge of life before the Cambrian explosion — the sudden of many kinds of animal fossils about 541 million years ago. After years of waiting. we are now getting our first glimpse of the only confirmed home of the Denisovans. Named after the Denisova cave in Siberia, where the ancient was found, these humans lived in Stone Age Eurasia alongs.de our species and the Neanderthals.

But groups would have included toddlers, pregnant women, older people and sick Ek•ople - and injury rates from hunting large animals at close quarters would have been high. Neanderthals cared for each other when sick or wDunded, and they a g sisted With childbirth. They probably dressed wounds — perhaps with lemming Hearth and home: fire the life Of Neanderthals. as it does for the San today skins, as the Inuit once did — and disinfected them with antiseptics including ochre. Their medical cabinet included painkillers and penicillin too. All this ministering implies that they had a place where they could remain sedentary — and safe — for extended "Home is that intimate place where you can feel supported and comforted and looked after," says Spikins.

Neanderthals buried their dead under the floor of their caves or shelters, something that H. sapiens were still doing much later in the Neolithic pericxi. Both groups also practised cannibalism, perhaps for ritual rather than "Rocks and bones were used to demarcate proto-rooms in Neanderthal homes" nutritional reasons — "rx'ssibly the ultimate caring act", says Gamble. Unlike their human Neanderthals don't seem to have buried their dead in the — another indication of the significance they attached to home.

We don 't know whether Neanderthals were the first homemakers. [here IS plenty of evidence that H. sapiens were building similar shelters and inhabiting rock dwellings at much the same time. Their open-air camps Scx»n took on an feel of semi-Ek•rmanence, unlike those of Neanderthals, who kept moving in a seasonal round. But Neanderthals often returned to favourite caves and once there they lit fires and bedded down where they always had. Gamble likens such behaviour to the well-worn gestures we all make on returning home — switching the lights on, drawing the curtains and so nn.

"There is a memory there," he says. "That sort of tehaviour is very like ours." One thing that has yet to be found in Neanderthal homes is anything resembling what is seen as artin the context of their H. sapiens contempraries. Mysterious arrangements of stalagmites were discovered two years ago in the pitch-black depthsofBruniquelcavein south-western France. Although created by Neanderthals, this seem to have been a living space. Meanwhile, is reluctant toattach the label "art" tothe large piles of mammoth bones his group found at a cave called La Cotte de Saint Brélade, a Neanderthal home In Jersey, In the channel Islands, even though some Of the piles are so well ordered it is tempting to meaning in their structure.

That doesn't signify that Neanderthals were incapable of symbolic thought. In 2018, Joäo Zilhäo at the University of Barcelona in Spain revealed that living in the Iberian peninsula painted caves at least 65,000 years ago and their own bodies at least 115.000 years ago. Perhaps they felt less need to broadcast their symtX)lism than modern humans did, or perhaps it took different forms and served different For example, it is possible, says Gamble, that the stalagmites in Bruniquel form a preh istoric xylophone on which Neanderthals made music.

For Zilhäo, the emerging story of Neanderthal domesticity is the logical culmination of the reassessment of who they were. They may have looked different, he says, but they were "just humans" living at a time when anatomical diversity among human groups was greater than it is tcxiay. Spikins agrees. The rethink Ik•gan with clues that they buried their dead, but the watershed came with the discovery that rncxlern humans and Neanderthals interbred, she says. "Suddenly it was much more acceptable to see their more humanlike qualities." All this firmly overturns the idea that Neanderthals were brutish.
"A more accurate reconstruction would come from The Flintstones," says Pope. Laura Spinney is a writer based in Paris, France 9 February 20191 NewScientist 131

The calendar can be brought roug,lly back in line with the solar year— 365.24 days — by addinga 13th "intercalary'" month every third year, meaning a total of six additional months are added over an 18-year period. It was 10 times as energetic as any previously seen erupting from Proxima Centauri and made the star just about visible from Earth with the naked eye — only to people with impeccable vision when the sky is completely dark (arxiv.orVabs/1804.02001).

The star is a red dwarf just 4-3 light years away from us with a planet called Proxima Centauri b orbiting in the habitable zone. In two years of data since the flare was spotted. the researchers have seen 23 more. They estimate that Proxima Centauri will emit up to five superflares each year.
